The Gaokao, which translates into the National College Entrance Examination in English, so in June, early June, for three days, over the course of six subjects, a student takes tests, and depending on his performance on the Gaokao, that would determine which school the student will go to, which college the student will go to. ## seg-0001 / 00:00:00-00:01:19 / SPEAKER_00

So this is a very exciting day because we are officially starting the Gay to Lease journalism course. Traditionally, we've understood journalism and research as this method of just collecting information, organizing it, and then expressing it. But then along came a man named Gay to Lease, and he transformed journalism, and he transformed the way we understood research. So we created something called literary journalism, which is the idea that journalism can be by itself be literature. But the Gay to Lease method is going to teach us how to be creative, how to be imaginative, and how to engage with reality and engage with people, because we don't teach you this in school. In fact, we teach you the opposite. Don't explore. Just do what the teacher tells you to do. Where did he learn this? Well, he learned this at home. The reason why is that his father was a tailor. His father was a tailor, and he had a tailoring business in New Jersey.

## seg-0035 / 00:40:19-00:41:13 / SPEAKER_01

We continue our analysis of the U.S.-Iran war. And in this war, there are three major questions that will determine the outcome of this war as well as the world afterwards. These three questions are, number one, will the U.S. launch a ground invasion? So, right now, the United States and Israel are primarily focused on an air war, striking Iran from a distance. In the past, we would call this siege warfare. And as long as it remains an air war, the United States can choose to de -escalate and withdraw from the Middle East. Whereas if they choose to withdraw from the Middle East, they would lose this war, but if they choose to launch a ground invasion, it would escalate very quickly and they would be trapped in Iran for the next five to 10 years. The Divine Comedy is the greatest literary masterpiece in human history. When Dante wrote it in about 1300, he called it La Commedia. And the reason why is that at this time in history, epic poetry was considered high or tragic. And it was written usually in Latin. But for Dante, what he really believed is that epic poetry should be democratic. It should be accessible to the people. That's why he called it La Commedia, low, okay? Which meant comedy. And so he wrote it in Tuscan, which is the language of Florence, where he lived. Latin was the language of the elite in Europe. He wanted to write it in Tuscan so that ordinary people around him could access it. And as a result, Dante is a great believer in democracy. So Homer, Dante, and Shakespeare were, in their own respective languages, the greatest poets. Because first and foremost, they believed that poetry should be accessible by the people.

### Where did transnational capital come from?

Audience: I just want to ask because you're talking about transnational capital and I think it was in one of your lectures before and maybe some research elsewhere that it goes back. Xueqin Jiang: Great question. Let me provide some history as we talk about transnational capital and where it comes from. Transnational capital, it's a recent phenomenon. I would say only in the past 500 years. It starts with the Protestant Reformation. What's happening is that at this time, the Catholic Church is in control. It's a very authoritarian society and so, it's a very authoritarian institution and it demands the complete obedience of all Christians. And its main mechanism of control is the idea of heaven and hell. If you obey the Catholic Church, you are sent to heaven and if you disobey the Catholic Church, you're sent to hell.

Basically, the Catholic Church, the main weapon they can use against people is excommunication. You're just abandoned by the church and you'll just burn in hell for all eternity. The Protestant Reformation was a response to the authoritarianism of the Catholic Church. And the main doctrine established at this time was called Calvinism, and he proposed the idea of double predestination. And his argument is screw the Catholic Church, the Catholic Church does not have the authority to send people to heaven and hell because God at the beginning of time, at the start of creation, has already decided who's going to heaven and hell.

It's called double predestination. Everything is decided at the beginning. It's all fate. It's all part of God's plan. And so this negates the authority of the Catholic Church because the Catholic Church does not have the authority now to decide who goes to heaven and hell. God has already decided. But now what this does is create a central dilemma in people: how do you know if you've been picked by God or not? Well, the obvious answer is well, it depends on how fortunate you have been in society. If you become very wealthy, that means that God favors you.

The way to resolve this fear and anxiety is to become rich. But once you become rich, you can't actually spend the money because otherwise you won't be virtuous. Otherwise God won't favor you. The idea of Calvinism is you have to become very rich and even richer to prove God favors you. And you can't spend the money, you can only invest it. And this creates the impetus for capitalism because this is unique in human history where now that you have money, you don't spend it, you just go invest it, you just go put it in the bank and this creates the modern financial system.

Because if you think about it, throughout most of human history, if you had money, the first thing you would do is give it to your friends and family because that's how you build status in your society. When the Vikings went to invade England and Ireland, they brought back all this gold, and then they gave it to their friends and had all these major feasts to celebrate because all they were interested in was the status that came from wealth, not the wealth itself. The Calvinists are unique in that they were only concerned about wealth itself and not the status that comes from wealth because wealth was their ticket into heaven.

Now, what happens is Calvinism gives birth to the Dutch Republic. The Dutch Republic becomes the wealthiest area of the world at this time because imagine a society where everyone is just obsessed with wealth accumulation. Well, it becomes very wealthy over time. The problem with the Dutch Republic though is well, they're wealthy, but the Spanish, the Habsburg Empire can come and just steal it from them. What they do is this. They make an arrangement with England where the Dutch Republic transfers their wealth to England for safekeeping. This is what we call the 1688 Glorious Revolution.

And as part of this agreement, they create something called the Bank of England, which is started in 1694. The Bank of England is unique because it's the first time in human history where all the private deposits, the private capital is guaranteed by the state, by Parliament. Before, if you were rich, you would lend money to a prince or a king to fight a war. That's problematic because the prince could die, the prince could say screw you, I'm not going to pay you back, or the prince could lose the war. It was very risky.

But if you're lending money to Parliament, to the nation-state, well, you have nothing to worry about. And this is what gives rise to the idea of transnational capital, where a nation will take money from overseas and the nation doesn't really care where the money comes from. It came from the Vatican, came from the Habsburg empire, it came from the Dutch Republic, it came from everywhere. Because at this time in history, England, because of its system, was considered the safest place to invest. And all this money would be guaranteed by the nation-state, by the people of this nation-state.

# Global Meet-Up #1 (Tokyo): Japan's Geo-Political Outlook

### What are my first impressions of Japan?

Five trains later, I'm getting frustrated. I'm like, “Regardless of how many people are on the train, I'm going to dive in.” There's 10 people around me. There are 10 guys around me. Train comes in, the carriage is full. I'm like, “There's no way we're getting into the train, but I'm sick of waiting.” We go, all 10 of us at the same time, get in the train, and for whatever reason, we all fit.

There's no conflict. It just happens miraculously. And we're like, “This is really strange.” That's my first experience with Japan.

I'm on my way from the airport to the hotel. I'm sitting, and I realize—and it's shocking to me—there's no beeping. We're on the highway. We're going really fast from the airport to the hotel, and there's just no beeping. I say to my friend who picked me up at the airport, and I ask her, “Why does no one beep in Japan?” And she's like, “Because it's bad manners.” And I'm like, “Yes, it is bad manners, but we beep all the time in China, so why is no one beeping in Japan?”

That's the second story. The third story is we get to the hotel, and a podcaster invited me to Japan, the Naokiman Podcast. They're paying for the hotel, but the hotel needs a credit card. I take out from my wallet my credit card and I give it to the hotel staff.

She comes back and says, “It says debit card.” And I'm like, “I know it says debit card, but it's a credit card, trust me.” She goes back to talk to her manager, and I can't understand why they come back and say, “It's a debit card.” I say, “It's both a debit card and a credit card.” And they're like, “It's a debit card.” I'm like, “It's a credit card, trust me.” After a bit, I'm like, “Fine, here's a credit card.” And they say, “Yes, thank you.”

Those are my three stories of Japan so far. The point is that these stories basically confirm to me my suspicions about Japan before I came here, which is that Japan is an extremely harmonious society, which is very cohesive and where people are able to synchronize just subconsciously. Think of the subway, the train story, where everyone knows how to fit into the train without actually coming into conflict with each other. That's very impressive.

At the same time, Japanese are very rules-obsessed, right? If you need a credit card, it can't be a debit card; it has to be a credit card. It can't be both a credit card and a debit card; it has to be a credit card. Those are my impressions of Japan so far.

## Japan’s development and East Asia

### How do I see Japan developing?

I was on a Naokiman podcast this afternoon. We talked for 3 hours. I basically laid out my understanding of what's happening in East Asia. I think that right now there are two major flashpoints in the world. You have the Middle East, you have Ukraine, and I think the third flashpoint will be East Asia.

I think East Asia will be the most complicated because you have some pretty sophisticated geopolitical actors in East Asia, including South Korea, North Korea, China, Japan, Taiwan, Philippines, Australia. It's a very complicated situation. But I'll just summarize for you what we really talked about.

The US strategy is to retreat or remove itself from providing security guarantees in East Asia. Because for the past 50–60 years, it's America that guaranteed peace in East Asia. And as a result, the East Asian economies have skyrocketed. They boomed these few decades.

But from the American perspective, that's not really sustainable because that means paying for the upkeep of 50,000 troops in South Korea, 50,000 troops for Japan. America doesn't really want to do that anymore.

America wants to retreat. And once America retreats, there will be two points of contention in East Asia. The first, of course, will be Taiwan. The Chinese strategy is to, over time, economically unify Taiwan. The idea is that as the global economy becomes worse and worse, Taiwan will become much more dependent on China. And this will lead ultimately to political reunification. That's the Chinese strategy.

From the Japanese perspective, that would be a disaster because if Taiwan were to reunify with China, this would create an embargo on Japan. Because Japan needs access to the resources of Southeast Asia. Taiwan would block Southeast Asia from Japan, and this would create long-term security issues for Japan. Japan cannot allow that.

Japan is very quickly remilitarizing, and we can see a lot of potential tension in the shipping lanes of Southeast Asia. But China doesn't actually want to engage with Japan. The Chinese strategic mentality is to avoid confrontation and to use other mechanisms, economic coercion, diplomacy, in order to resolve military disputes.

I think the Chinese strategy will be to use North Korea as a point of leverage. The idea is, you're North Korea, and you're poor, but because you're poor, you have nothing to lose in this game, right? North Korea threatens South Korea with artillery, and then North Korea would lob missiles in the Sea of Japan. This would create a lot of crises in East Asia, in which case Japan would need to negotiate with China in order to keep North Korea at bay. That's the Chinese strategy.

And the Japanese strategy would be—Japan is actually in a lot of trouble, because there are three major issues.

The first major issue is the aging crisis. Every developed nation in the world faces an aging crisis, but Japan is far ahead of the curve. Japan is aging faster than other nations. And this is causing a lot of problems for Japan, especially immigration, right? If you have to bring immigrants in order to keep the economy going.

The second major issue is Japan is not self-sufficient in the way that the United States and China are self-sufficient. Japan is very dependent on imports and exports to feed its economy, to feed its people, basically.

And the third issue is that Japan has a lot of historical enemies in East Asia. Historically, Japan has had feuds with the Korean Peninsula, with China, with Southeast Asia. The geopolitical outlook is not great for Japan.

I think that the next 10 years will be critical for Japan. Because either Japan solves its demographic crisis right now, or at least in 10 years, basically its aging crisis—if it does not solve this problem in the next 10 years, I think Japan will cease to exist as a nation-state in 50 years' time. That's how serious this problem is. The aging crisis is a huge problem in Japan.

What I said in the podcast, and we can talk about this, is what Japan is facing is a stark choice that other nations won't face, but which Japan has to resolve by itself.

I think Japan, in the next 10 years, will attempt to resolve its demographic crisis by introducing mass euthanasia . That's our prediction. I think Japan will be forced into making this choice, where the only way for the nation to survive is by encouraging those who are over 80 to do euthanasia. And I don't see any other path. It's either Japan makes this choice or Japan ceases to exist in 50 years' time. And this is something we debate.

We're joking on a podcast, because we are talking. And I was joking that the solution is to get these old people to use psychedelics. If they use psychedelics, they will see that death is actually meaningless. And this is something that has a lot of validity because we know people who have near-death experiences. And after they die, they recognize that: “You know what? Death is just the beginning.”

There are also people who have cancer. And for the longest time, they were just dreading death. But the moment they start using psychedelics as part of their therapy, they start to be more welcoming. They start to be more open-minded about the possibility of death. They don't have fear of death.

The moment you start to lose the fear of death is the moment that you live life to your fullest. It may mean that you die, but it also means that before you die, you are really motivated to make the best of your time. You spend more time with your family. You spend more time doing what you love rather than just dreading.

## The aging crisis and the transfer of power

### What happens if Japan does not resolve aging crisis?

The first comment is we know exactly what would happen if this trend continues, where the elite are getting older and older and they refuse to surrender power.

What's going to happen is something called rat utopia. And this was an experiment conducted by John Calhoun in the '60s and '70s . Basically, he was interested in population growth and what it would mean for society if you have abundance. What would abundance mean for humanity?

He created this experiment where he took a room and turned it into a colony for rats. And in this room, he created a paradise: just free water, free food every day, no predators. These rats could just do whatever they wanted. And then he put these rats in this colony.

He tried this experiment for dozens of times. And every single time, it ended with a mass extinction of the colony. All the rats ended up dying. The reason why was, in nature, male rats fight over breeding rights. And the strongest rat, the alpha rat, gets to have his wife and they have children. And the other rats run off to start their own colonies or die out in nature. This is survival of the fittest, basically. And that's just the rule of nature.

But in this scenario, ratopia, no one dies. And even though the alpha male rats are able to beat up the other rats, the other rats have no place to go. They just hang out together. And eventually, they gang up on the alpha male rat. The alpha male rat will protect his family, but eventually he's just so sick of fighting rats over and over, he just runs away.

Then the other rats come and rape the female rat. And then the female rat is so sick of fighting off these rats that she loses her mind and she starts attacking her own children. And then these children run off, and because there's no adult protection, they also join this feral group of rats. And then you have gang warfare.

This is what happens to society if this trend continues, where the boomers refuse to give up power. Just imagine a scenario where you have a lot of young men, and right now they distract themselves with OnlyFans and Bitcoin and JPEGs and pornography, right? But eventually you reach a point where they form into groups, and that was just urban warfare. It's a civil war throughout.

Eventually society's like, “Screw this. We're going to send these men off to die in war in order to maintain social stability.” You destroy your society by killing off the young. But that's the only path forward if you don't allow the proper transfer of power from the old to the young. This society will die out.

This is something that every major industrial country faces today. Not just Japan, but China, the United States, Canada, Australia, Europe, everyone.

I think that my analysis of Japan is that it would have a cultural resilience to resolve this issue. Because the trick for the future is not to actually win wars. You can't do that nowadays with nuclear weapons. The trick is to maintain cultural cohesion and that mentality. That means the old have to surrender power to the young.

And only in Japan, I think, could that happen. I'm not saying it will happen. I'm saying, of all these societies I see, I think only Japan could pull this off. And if Japan pulls this off, then I can see Japan becoming a superpower of East Asia. It's the most pressing problem for humanity. That's our first point.

The second point is, why is this happening? Why is it that the old refuse to share the power? And we've never had a situation like this in human history before.

Primarily because we never had so much peace and prosperity before in human history. It was impossible for the old to live this long. But now that they're 80, 90—Chuck Grassley is 90 years old—what if they just retire and give it to someone who is more capable?

I think the answer is because we've adopted an extremely materialistic worldview which worships individual achievement. We worship people like Elon Musk or even a trillionaire, but we also worship people who live to 100 years old. It's like, “Wow, what an amazing individual achievement.”

In a lot of places, if you live to 100 years old, you get a visit by the mayor, there's a parade for you. You're celebrated. And you should be celebrated for living to 100 years old. But we don't think about the cost of having people live this long.

We adopted this extremely materialistic worldview that is competitive, that is individualistic, that is extremely selfish. And we reward people for that.

I think the only solution moving forward is to adopt a much more nationalistic, much more religious worldview. Which is to say, it's probably good to sacrifice yourself for the greater good. It's a noble thing to think of community before you think of the individual. But again, of all the societies that I see around me, China, the United States, Europe, I think only Japan can pull this off.

### Will porn-addicted young men really revolt?

It is very true that the young people seem apathetic today. It seems as though they're no longer interested in politics, they're no longer angry. It seems as though the internet has been able to channel a lot of their anger away. They spend a lot of time watching porn, playing video games, and apparently that has sort of dissipated their natural anger.

I think that's incorrect. We have to use a longer time horizon. The example I would use is the 1844 revolutions, which really destroyed old Europe. And what sparked the revolution was famine. It was climate change, wet weather, which caused the potato famine. It caused a lot of starvation, and that's when the entire society started to burn.

The idea that today, the young people can just watch porn online and get food delivered to them using Uber Eats—yeah, sure. But let's imagine a scenario where the global supply chain chokes up. And they're not going to be able to access food. Now that they're hungry, now that the economy has collapsed around the world, now I think they're angry.

And the Strait of Hormuz—it's a huge issue, and no one really appreciates what this really means for the global supply chain and the global food supply. Because, sure, the Strait of Hormuz, a lot of energy passes through that, but you know what? A lot of fertilizer passes through that as well.

About 20% of the world's fertilizer goes through that. Most of the world depends on fertilizer, especially the Global South. Imagine a scenario where there's famine in Africa, and it's going to have huge repercussions for the world, because then you have this mass migration into Europe. And this is going to be a sick society.

The thing about history is once a spark starts, every place gets ignited. I think it's easy to say, “We're special and we've solved the food problem. We've solved the abundance issue, so we're going to be immune from history.” I would disagree.

I think the entire world that we live in is much more fragile than we think. Can you imagine, 2 years ago, the United States would be striking Iran, fighting this pointless war, destroying the global economy? They got access to oil. It would have been unimaginable 2 years ago. I think 2 years from now, the world will be much more unimaginable.

## Japan’s cultural resilience and work ethic

### Can Japan change?

I think that if you look at the global supply chain, Southeast Asia is particularly vulnerable. The reason why is you have a lot of people in Southeast Asia, not enough resources. Places like Indonesia, Malaysia, are going to face a lot of political turbulence for the next 10–20 years.

If we focus on Japan, it seems Japan is in the worst-case scenario because Japan is heavily industrialized, but it's also heavily dependent on global trade, especially on energy from the Middle East, and also food from other places.

I think that Japan will be one of the first industrial nations to suffer the major repercussions and consequences of the Strait of Hormuz closure. And you will have a lot of problems in Japan.

But I think that once these problems arise, once Japan recognizes how stark the future is, then I think that Japan will make some important changes that were previously unimaginable. And Japan will prove much more culturally resilient and flexible than other places. And I think it's probably because the situation in Japan is particularly stark. And that's point one.

Point two is, as the United States retreats from the Pacific theater, the United States sees Japan as its major proxy. Because the United States is interested in divide and rule. Before, it could use divide and conquer to control the world, but now it cannot, because a lot of nations refuse to submit to American power. Now America is forced to use divide and conquer. And as a result, America will protect Japan. Because at the end of the day, the Western Hemisphere is extremely rich. Japan won't have to suffer a food or oil crisis because they can continue to import this from the Western Hemisphere.

But I think that as a culture, as a people, the Japanese will also recognize that it's probably not a good idea to be completely dependent on America in the long term. And it's probably important to diversify and make some social changes to adapt to the new reality. I don't think the future in Japan is as bleak as people would imagine it to be.

### Why am I hopeful about Japan?

What I'll say is this. Young people throughout the world, especially in industrial economies, they no longer want to work, right? America, young people, they could choose to work in factories. There are lots of manufacturing jobs in America that pay really well. They don't want to do that. They would rather take whatever meager savings they have and go and gamble on cryptocurrencies.

The expectations and attitudes and the values of the young people are really skewed. Maybe before, my generation, to make 80,000 a year working as an engineer was considered really prestigious. Now the young people, if you ask them, “What do you want to do? And how much money do you want to make?” Their average expectation is to work as a social media influencer, like me, making 600,000 a year. And then, which I probably got when I was 21 years old, right? It's insane what their expectations are. This is a problem throughout the world.

The thing I will say about Japan is that, for whatever reason, there's still a sense of conscientiousness in Japan, where if they do something, they want to do it well.

You don't really see that anymore around the world. I'm from China, I live in China. And people don't take their work seriously. Even if Japan has problems, it's nowhere as bad as anywhere else. And I think a lot of it has to do with the cultural cohesion, where people would feel embarrassed if they didn't do a good job. They'd rather not work rather than do a bad job.

But in China and the United States, you have a lot of attitude where, in China, we have a phrase called “bai lan,” which is “let it rot.” Rather than do a good job, just do a terrible job because that's what other people deserve.

In China, it's really strange, but the attitude is: to express your individuality, to express your autonomy and agency, do a really crappy job. 'Cause that's the only way to rebel against the system. Whereas I don't think that this would ever happen in Japan.

## Taiwan, China, and the United States

### Will China invade Taiwan?

Taiwan—Japan would absolutely get involved in the war, because again, Japan sees Taiwan as vital to its core national security interests. Because Taiwan would block Japan from accessing Southeast Asia. And this would hurt Japan in the long term, strategically. But I think the chance of China actually invading Taiwan is extremely minuscule. And a lot of this has to do with Chinese geopolitical thinking.

What I can say is the Americans play chess, which is direct, logical, and confrontational. Chinese play Go, which is indirect and long-term and very patient.

China doesn't like military conflicts. China does whatever it can to avoid direct military confrontation. An example is Iran, where the only reason why Iran would agree to a ceasefire is China applied a lot of the pressure on Iran. Go back to mid-April or April when the ceasefire was announced.

We didn't expect them to close the Strait of Hormuz. We didn't expect them to attack GCC energy infrastructure. We weren't prepared for this.

Clearly America was on the back foot. Iran had a strategic advantage. Why stop the war? And the reason why you stopped the war is China says, “You guys stop the war because you're hurting the economy too much. You're hurting our economy.” And China buys 90% of Iranian oil, so that's a lot of pressure.

But the way China does this is interesting. China didn't come out and say, “We don't support this war or whatever.” China got Pakistan to come in to be the mediator. That's how China operates. It's always behind the scenes. It's always back channels.

China does not like confrontation. It creates a lot of issues for China. There's a lot of Chinese strategic texts, like Sun Tzu's Art of War and Romance of the Three Kingdoms , that determine how Chinese perceive strategy. That's point one. China does not like military confrontation.

Point number two is, right now there is a political shift in Taiwan. There's a very charismatic chairwoman of the KMT, the opposition party in Taiwan, named Cheng Li-wun. And she's been saying:

Why is there a fight between China and Taiwan? We're just one big family.

And that's point two.

Point three is the Americans actually are encouraging reunification between Taiwan and China. Just think about game theory and how I would behave if I'm Donald Trump. This is commercial.

If I'm America, I'm like, “Fine, you unify.” What do I lose? I lose nothing.

China does not benefit at all from invading Taiwan. It may not even win militarily. That's the issue. Why take this huge chance when, over time, Taiwan and China want to reunify naturally?

### Will Trump sell out Taiwan?

Why would the United States give up Taiwan? And the reason why is Trump is transactional. He doesn't have any ideology. Taiwan's democratic, who cares? What can I trade Taiwan for? That's all he cares about, right? And because Taiwan is the ultimate national goal of China, China's actually willing to sacrifice a lot for Taiwan.

Geopolitically, about America, I don't really lose that much by surrendering Taiwan. Remember what happened. Trump visits China and then there's some secret meetings. And then after the meeting, Trump says to a reporter:

## The roots of Japanese cohesion

### Why is Japan so cohesive?

I think there's certain explanations or certain reasons to compel Japanese cohesion. The first is that, for the longest time, China was sort of gravity in East Asia. Japan always felt threatened by China, not just militarily, but culturally as well. If you're Japan, how do you distinguish yourself culturally from China? Because you obviously don't want to be colonized culturally by China. That's the first impetus for cohesion.

The second thing is the continuity of the culture. You look at China, China doesn't have any continuous culture. This is a great misunderstanding of China. The last ethnic Chinese dynasty was the Han dynasty in about the year 500. After that, most Chinese were ethnic minorities.

The Tang dynasty were not ethnic Chinese. They were what we call the Xianbei zu, which is a Turkish people. But they disguised themselves as Chinese to better rule the people.

Obviously, if you're ethnic Chinese, as opposed to if you are a minority, you're going to govern the country differently. If you are ethnic Chinese, you believe in greater China. You believe that it is China's destiny to expand outwards. And that's what the Han did.

But if you are an ethnic minority, what you're first and foremost concerned about is maintaining your rule over the people. You want to maintain a more insular foreign policy. And that's what the Tang did.

## Spain Defeats Argentina

There are different possibilities.

The first possibility is that I am just paranoid, everyone is paranoid, none of this is rigged, and the world is not as deterministic as we once believed. My entire framework for understanding the world could be completely off base. That is a very strong possibility.

The second possibility is that they rigged the tournament up to a point. They wanted four teams in the semifinals because these four teams would draw the most revenue for FIFA: Spain, France, England, and Argentina. That is what they got. They did not really care what happened in the final.

The third possibility is that they did rig it, but Argentina became too arrogant. It suffered from hubris and underperformed.

Argentina became the first team in a World Cup final not to have a shot on goal in the first 90 minutes. In fact, I think Argentina got its first shot on goal around the 120-minute mark. Spain outplayed Argentina throughout.

The first tough team it faced was England in the semifinal, so it became lazy and complacent and did not perform to the best of its ability.

These are three possibilities. I am not saying which one is correct. I am saying that all three are possibilities we should consider.

What I do is try to develop predictive models for the world. It is always important to step back and ask what our framework, assumptions, and predictions are, and then analyze in real time how those predictions turn out.

To be fair to myself, I never said Argentina would win. What I said was that if Argentina won, if it was clear that the officials were rigging the game in Argentina’s favor, and if Messi scored the winning goal, then I would predict that Messi would become president of Argentina in five to ten years and that Argentina would become a major hub of transnational capital.

I see myself as a teacher of the world. I feel extremely privileged to be in this position, but I also appreciate that this privilege comes with a lot of responsibilities. I apologize if I misled people in the past. I will try my very best to be more nuanced, subtle, and balanced.

## Do Predictions Change Outcomes?

### Now that people are paying attention to your predictions, could making a prediction change the outcome?

In theory, making these predictions should influence the outcome, but my intuition tells me that is not the case.

I used to play a lot of Texas hold ’em poker. At a table of ten people, there might be only two people in a hand. Sometimes a hand becomes really intense and goes on for half an hour because it is the river card, a major bet has been made, and one of the players is forced to think deeply about whether to call or fold.

The other people at the table are more objective observers. They can possibly make better decisions than the people in the hand because they are neutral and can observe how both players are playing.

But never in my life have I seen an instance in which the actions or talking of the spectators influenced the decision-making of the people in the hand. The people in the hand tend to block everything else out.

In theory, if I am making these predictions, perhaps the players in the game will take them into account. But in my observation, people do not really care what observers think or want. They focus on the game itself.

If more of the world’s population becomes aware of what is happening, perhaps that awareness will eventually affect decision-makers and cause them to play the game differently. We will see.

## Jews, the Catholic Church, and Medieval Europe

### Why did Jews, especially rabbis, agree to be repeatedly abused and scapegoated by the Catholic Church?

The history of Judaism in Europe after Christianity is very complicated.

After the rise of Christianity and Islam, many Jews converted to both religions. The first Christians—people such as Paul, Peter, and Jesus—were Jews.

Judaism became a minority religion. Before Christianity, Jews made up around 10% of the Roman Empire. That is a lot of people. In Alexandria, around a third of the population was Jewish.

Jews were a huge cultural force during the Roman Empire. With the rise of Christianity and Islam, they became a much smaller minority.

During the Middle Ages, there were still pockets of Jews around Europe. This history is not fully appreciated.

There were many pogroms, persecutions, and instances of Jews being used as scapegoats, especially during the worst economic periods. But for much of this history, Jews were treated better than people appreciate.

There were two main powers in Europe: the feudal nobility and the Catholic Church.

A Christian lord or noble was not allowed to lend money at interest, but Jews could do it. You had the Jews act as the scapegoat.

For most of history, this relationship worked. Jews accumulated wealth and gave a huge portion of it to the nobles. They worked hard and provided access to trade in the Islamic caliphate.

From the perspective of the nobility, this was a great relationship. Jews accepted it because it allowed them to practice their religion and remain together as a community.

The Jews became that alien other.

For most of the time, this relationship worked well for the Catholic Church, the nobility, and the Jews.

They diverted popular attention toward the Jews. They planted spies and agents within peasant uprisings and directed the peasants’ anger toward Jewish communities.

## Spirituality, Eschatology, and God

I have a lot of issues with eschatology. My main theory is that we have eschatology because of Proto-Indo-European religion.

Proto-Indo-European religion is unique in human history because it was the first systematic religion to believe that violence created the universe.

Before the Proto-Indo-Europeans, most traditions subscribed to an animistic or mother-goddess understanding. They believed in the balance and harmony of the world and that we were all part of the mother goddess and part of nature.

The Proto-Indo-Europeans were imperialistic. They believed violence created the world.

The most basic Proto-Indo-European myth begins with twins. One twin has to kill the other to found the world.

This myth becomes a template for the Roman religion, in which Romulus has to kill Remus to found Rome. It also becomes foundational for many other religions, especially the Abrahamic religions.

If you believe that the world was created through violence, you also have to believe that the world must end through violence. That is why you have eschatology.

The Proto-Indo-Europeans gave us both Zoroastrianism and Judaism. Over time, both became extremely eschatological.

The world does not necessarily need to be eschatological. Unfortunately, we are controlled by people who believe in eschatology.

Before, if you were rich, you would lend money to a prince or a king to fight a war. That's problematic because the prince could die, the prince could say screw you, I'm not going to pay you back, or the prince could lose the war. It was very risky.

Professor Jiang: Capitalism is a historical accident. I know that most of you believe that capitalism is just the best way to run the world. But what I want to show you is that, in fact, it's a convergence of several historical accidents that has created the world that we live in today.

The first historical accident is Calvinism. In Calvinism, there's a very important idea called double predestination. In double predestination, the idea is, at the beginning of time, when God created the universe, he already decided the destiny of everyone. He already decided who is going to go to heaven and who will go to hell. Double meaning heaven and hell; predestination means it's already been decided.

Why we have double predestination was it was a rhetorical response to the Catholic Church. The Catholic Church was able to control people because the Catholic Church could determine whether or not you went to heaven or hell. That was the source of their power. Calvinism was trying to subvert the power by saying, “No, the church doesn't have this power. Only God has this power, and God has already decided.”

No matter what you do, no matter what the church says, your fate has already been decided. At this point in history, indulgences were a huge problem. Indulgences were just bribes to the church so that, if you're a bad rich person, you could basically get to heaven still.

What's really interesting is Calvinism creates a moral dilemma that didn't exist before, which is, how do you know if God has chosen you or not? Before, you would know because the church would tell you if you were selected or not. But now you have to believe if you're chosen or not. The way they remedied this is through the idea of wealth creation. Basically, if you're wealthy, it means God favors you. That makes sense, right?

But the other thing that's interesting is Calvinism demanded that you make wealth, but at the same time also not spend your wealth, because you have to prove you are a good person, right? You make a lot of wealth, but you can't even spend your wealth. This goes against human intuition because, historically, when we make a lot of money, the first thing we do is spend it on our friends and family, right? We take this wealth, and we transfer it into status for ourselves in a community. That's what intuitively we did in the past.

But now Calvinism breaks this cycle and says, “No, no, no. If you make a lot of money, you also have to save it,” which basically means you have to invest it. This is weird, but this basically creates capitalism. You can't spend your money. You can only save it.

Because of this concept, you now have a new entity in the world called the Dutch Republic. What the Dutch Republic would do is take people's savings and then start these enterprises around the world that led to a spice monopoly. At this time in history, spices are the most valuable thing in the world. The Dutch Republic, because of Calvinism, now becomes the wealthiest region in the world, and they create really the world's first idea of a middle class. This leads, of course, to something called the Dutch Renaissance.

The problem with this is the Dutch Republic used to be part of the Habsburg Empire, and now that they're so wealthy, they're constantly being invaded. You have all this money. You have to protect this money in order to get to heaven. That's your ticket to heaven. But how do you prevent the Catholics from coming and stealing your money?

This led to something called the Glorious Revolution: 1688, Glorious Revolution. This is the second historical accident. The Glorious Revolution is really a marriage of the dominant Protestant powers in Europe at this time, which are England and the Dutch Republic. With the Glorious Revolution, what happens is the Dutch Republic now transfers their gold, their wealth, to England. Why? Because England is an island protected by the Royal Navy. The Royal Navy is invincible, right? It's really the best place to store your money.

The Glorious Revolution then leads to the chartering of the Bank of England. This is the third historical accident: the Bank of England, 1694.

The Bank of England is unique in history because it's run by merchants, right? Historically, merchants would lend money to kings for their wars. The problem is the kings could die. They could lose the war. Or they could be like, “Screw you. I'm the king. I don't have to pay you back.” This was always a huge problem for these merchants.

The Bank of England solved this problem because they're lending money not to the king but to Parliament. Basically, the Bank of England—and, again, it's so weird if you think about it—is a private bank that is guaranteed by the people of England. Now you're lending money not to the king but to the English nation, which basically means that as long as there's one Englishman alive, that person has to pay you back.

It's a really weird system, but this creates our modern financial system. The Bank of England model, of course, will be copied with the Federal Reserve. The Federal Reserve system in the United States is modeled on the Bank of England system.

This system is great because what it allows is basically infinite financing. The example is the Napoleonic Wars, when England was trying to fight Napoleon for dominance in Europe, and England lost six times. It only won once, but England only needed to win once because it has infinite financing. No matter how badly Napoleon defeated them on the battlefield, England could just print money and say, “We'll bribe you Prussians or Russians to go fight another war.”

The Bank of England basically creates the British Empire. Then what happens, of course, is these ideas will then spread to the United States and create the American Empire.

### Question: What makes you believe in God or the Monad?

### Question: Why compare the next 50 years to the Bronze Age collapse?

Questioner: Across multiple podcasts, and in this lecture too, you alluded to a Bronze Age-type collapse in the next 50 years. First of all, what's the probability, in your honest opinion, of that actually happening? Number two, what will actually happen that you compare it to the Bronze Age collapse and not to something like the Great Depression or after World War II?

Professor Jiang: My logic is very simple. Right now, there are 8 billion people in the world, and these 8 billion people all want to live, right? They all want to survive. The problem is we are able to support 8 billion people because of access to cheap energy, mainly from the Middle East.

If you remove the GCC from the equation, let's pretend the GCC doesn't even exist, you would lose access to fertilizer—not all fertilizer, but a lot of fertilizer. You lose access to cheap energy. Then there's a possibility of famine in Africa, of social revolution throughout Europe.

What people don't appreciate about the Bronze Age collapse is things were perfectly normal until they weren't. If you lived during the Bronze Age, you would think, “Wow, we live in a perfect world because everything is interconnected.” You assume that this interconnection leads to resilience. It leads to dexterity, but it's the opposite. It actually leads to fragility. If there's one problem that arises somewhere, it cascades across the entire world.

Again, I hate to say this, but you've got 8 billion people, and there are only resources enough to support 2 billion people. This includes water and food, right? What are people going to do? You have kids, and you're in Africa, and there's not enough food and water. What do you do? You migrate, right? You migrate. You join bands of pirates, bandits, because that's the best way to survive. Then you become an army, right? Then you try to overwhelm the defense of Europe, which leads to wars. This is what happened during the Bronze Age.

Migration is going to be a huge problem in this world over the next 10 years because there's not enough food to feed people. Famine is going to be a huge issue, and this will lead to war. This is not World War III. This is a breakdown of civilization.

When this happens, when people don't have enough to eat, human decency goes out the window. “I don't care that you're a human being. You have food. You have water, and I need it from you, so I'm going to kill you.” It's either you—it's dog-eat-dog, right?

Questioner: Do you think that's engineered too?

Professor Jiang: I think it's the path of least resistance, right? “I don't want it to happen, but if it happens, I have a bunker in New Zealand. I have a helicopter that can transport me to somewhere else. I have this mansion in the Pacific Palisades, and I can build a fortress.” It's the path of least resistance. I think these people in charge, the problem is not that they're evil, the problem is they're just—

If the teacher can say, “I am wrong,” that gives permission to the student to say, “I can be wrong as well, and I should just accept I can be wrong, and then learn from my mistakes and improve.” That's the greatest gift you can ever give to your students.

### Question: How does free will relate to personal tragedies?

Professor Jiang: That's a really good question. Again, we all come here for our own individual experience, and why we've come is something that is unique to us. I think that I came with a specific purpose of trying to enlighten others, and that means, first of all, seeking self-enlightenment. That can only be done through personal tragedy and personal trauma. Professor Jiang: That's right.

Professor Jiang: I've been a teacher for my entire adult life, and for the longest time I was not reaching people. People thought I was crazy. But once you go through it, you can never go back, right? Then you're happier for it.

# Global Meet-Up #2 (Los Angeles): The “End of the World” US Tour

What I want to do today is basically provide a framework for understanding how we got to this point and where we're going.

## First impressions of Los Angeles

To start, I want to tell you my first impressions of Los Angeles. It's my first time here, and Theo Von invited me to be on this podcast . I came in Wednesday, and they put me in West Hollywood, a very nice place, a really beautiful hotel.

I enjoy walking around the city to get a sense of the culture. I was walking around the Sunset Boulevard area, and the residential area is just beautiful. I'm just admiring the houses, the sunlight, the beauty of it all, and then I see, right in the middle of the pavement, a pile of dog shit. I obviously walk around it. It takes me a couple of minutes before I realize it probably didn't come from a dog.

That's my first impression of LA, unfortunately.

Then my next impression of LA is I went to breakfast, and I went to the cheapest place I could find. I paid $17 for avocado on toast. $17 on avocado on toast. I was like, “There better be cocaine in this thing.” Unfortunately, there wasn't.

I've been walking around the city. There's really a lot of homeless people. There's a lot of drug addicts. The impression that I've developed these past three days is America is suffering from imperial exhaustion . It's an empire really in decline. It's exhausted.

When I was in China, I would just hear Americans talk great things about China. I live in China, and I see all the problems. I really didn't understand why Americans thought China was great until I came here and see the world from your perspective. Honestly, from your perspective, everything is great.

## Bretton Woods and the US dollar system

Let me give some historical background as to how we got to this point. The year is 1944, and America is about to win this war against Japan and Germany. They organize the Bretton Woods conference in New Hampshire, and the idea is to establish the US dollar as a world reserve currency.

The logic of this is very simple. In World War II, America had to build a lot of factories to supply armaments for its war machine. Now that the war is coming to an end, what do you do with these factories? The answer is you turn these factories from manufacturing munitions and weapons to manufacturing TVs, cars for the global market.

The problem is the entire world is destroyed because of World War II. What America did was lend the world the money in order to buy cars and washing machines and television sets. This became the basis for Pax Americana as well as the US dollar system.

Because America was lending so much money to Europe and to Japan, it needed collateral for this financing, and this collateral, of course, was gold. The agreement was that US dollars would always be pegged to gold. We call this a gold standard, and it worked great for the first 10, 20 years because it allowed the average American middle-class person to live like a Roman emperor.

If you were a white male in the 1950s, you were in paradise. You had maybe a factory job, but with that factory job, you could have your wife work at home. You could raise three kids and have them all go to college. You could go on vacation twice a year. You had two cars. It really was the best life.

Unfortunately, America started to waste a lot of this, what we call exorbitant privilege, the right to print US dollars. America started to do stupid things, like, for example, the war in Vietnam, the space race, the Great Society. At this point, the world recognized that maybe America is spending too much money.

At the same time, the rest of the world is catching up to America industrially. Germany and Japan were devastated in the war, but they're working really hard, and now their industrial capacity is surpassing that of the United States. What's happened is America went from a creditor nation to a debtor nation. That's bad because you owe everyone gold, and there's not enough gold in the world to pay off the debt.

What happens is in 1971, Richard Nixon declares, “Remember how in 1944 we agreed that US dollars would be pegged to gold? The gold standard? Well, forget about it. From now on, the US dollar, it's all free-floating. It's just fiat currency. We will not give you gold for US dollars.”

Now this creates a crisis of confidence, and to resolve this crisis of confidence, Nixon does two things. He visits Saudi Arabia and agrees to get them to sell oil only in US dollars. We call this the petrodollar. The other thing that he does is he goes to China and gets China to start to liberalize its economy, to start working in the United States. Basically, what China does is use its cheap labor in order to manufacture goods for the global economy and sell its cheap labor in US dollars.

These two things, what happened in the Middle East and what happened in East Asia, now become the new framework for the global economy. The idea is that the Middle East will sell its oil to East Asia so that Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China could then make manufactured goods to sell the world. All this is being facilitated in US dollars. All this money, because it's being facilitated in US dollars, goes back to America.

Because of this global system, America now has to shift from a manufacturing power to a financial power in order to process all this trade. This has led to the financialization, the hollowing out of the American manufacturing sector. This has led to tremendous problems in American society.

For one thing, it's led to tremendous inequality. Another thing is that America now is forced to provide security guarantees for the entire world, so its military is overextended. This is what is called imperial overstretch. Another thing that happens is there's so much power in the financial sector that it leads to corruption.

This is what obviously led to the 2008 subprime crisis because you got these Wall Street banks out of control, and they were all engaged in speculation. They didn't really care because they knew that, no matter what happened, the government would pick up the tab at the end of the day. They engaged in all this reckless behavior, and this has led to the world that we live in today.

Obama was elected in 2008 to fix these issues, to represent the working class. But he didn't do that. That's why in 2016 we got Donald Trump, who promised to build a wall to stop illegal immigration. He also promised to basically prevent the world from taking advantage of America. This has led to the Trump years.

## The causes of imperial decline

### Is this preordained or a series of political accidents?

Question:

One of the things that I always wonder about is how much of what we're seeing now is preordained versus a series of political accidents, like Trump getting elected the first time, Brexit. It feels as though we were almost two elections away from avoiding all of this. But when I watch your lectures, I feel like this was almost preplanned, preordained.

Answer:

I would say we are in an age of imperial decline. If you look at history, empires decline for very much the same reasons, and the pattern of decline is very similar. I will say there are three major causes of American imperial decline.

The first is financialization. Thomas Piketty talks about this in his book Capital in the Twenty-First Century , where, as capitalism progresses, eventually you reach a point where it's much more lucrative to do financial speculation than it is to do real wealth creation.

Let's just imagine you're an entrepreneur, and you work really hard, like Ally, and you create a lot of wealth. You hire a lot of people, and now you have a lot of savings. What you do with these savings is you invest in other enterprises. You engage in financial speculation, and what you realize is, “Wow, financial speculation is a lot more profitable than real wealth creation, like opening a business.”

This is just how capitalism works. Thomas shows that, over time, just the logic of capitalism, because it is really the consolidation of capital in the hands of really smart investors, then stock market speculation will be a lot more lucrative than real wealth creation.

The example he gives is, on average, if you put your money in the stock market, you might get 5% returns. If you open a restaurant or open a factory, you might get a 2% return a year. Eventually, you reach a point where, “I'm not going to go open a restaurant or start a business. I'll just spend my money in the stock market.” That's where we are today. It's much more lucrative to go play the stock market or cryptocurrency than it is to open a factory. That's number one.

Number two is you also have the bureaucratization of society, meaning that these bureaucracies that were meant to coordinate and centralize resources become bigger and bigger over time until they become parasites.

The classic example is our universities. If you go to a university in the 1950s, it was really about making sure the professors could teach well and do research. Administrators were just professors who volunteered four years of their time. Professors would become university president for four years, then return to teaching and research. That was true for most administrative faculties.

Now the administration of universities is a full-time bureaucracy. Quite honestly, there's more of them than there are professors. Because there's so many of them, they're always causing problems in order to justify their existence. That's why we have DEI and political correctness and student-centered learning, because they want the students to complain in order to justify their existence.

That's why it's almost impossible as a professor to teach, because if a student complains, a dean's going to come to you and spend the next few months investigating the complaint, even though the complaint may be completely warrantless.

There's a huge problem in universities. A lot of the reason why is bureaucracies expand because bureaucrats have children, and they need to put their children somewhere. It's often in the bureaucracy. That's why bureaucracies expand over time. This, again, is a pretty consistent pattern in human history.

The third thing that's driving all this is the idea of elite overproduction. There's a civil war going on between the Wall Street financial elite, which has controlled America since the Clinton–Obama years, and now you have the Silicon Valley tech oligarchs who are trying to wrest control over policymaking in Washington, DC.

In 2008, because the financial elite were able to control Washington, DC, they could force a bailout. Now what Sam Altman and other techs want to do is basically get Trump to nationalize data centers so the cost of AI shifts to the government. Basically, government subsidies for Sam Altman and his brethren.

That is why empires decline over time, these three reasons. You have financialization, bureaucratization, and then you also have elite overproduction.

Now, it does seem there is some coordination going on. The reason why is these secret societies, because they practice the occult, they have an understanding of tens of thousands of years of human history. They understand the broad scope, the broad pattern of human history, and so they're able to anticipate events.

Not only do they do that, but what they recognize is, “We can't control the course of human events, but by working together, we can accelerate the course of human events.” Why is that important? Because we stand to make a lot of money doing this. The financial system will collapse, but if we can control when it will collapse, we will make all the money. It's going to collapse sooner or later, but if we're able to pick the right time when it collapses, then we will make a killing.

That's why they're so interested in astrology and eschatology and all these things. In many ways, it does seem coordinated, but we have to remember that these people are first and foremost accelerationists. They cannot change the course of events, but they can accelerate the course of events.

We're already seeing this where you look at the Trump years, and this past year he's done what many presidents will do in about 10 years. We are seeing so much change these past few months. The reason why is we are really at the end of empire. What they're trying to do is they're trying to accelerate the collapse of empire and then basically create the conditions for a new empire to arise, whether it be in Israel or Argentina or China. They're trying to accelerate events so as to maximize their profit.

## Bretton Woods and the US dollar system

Let me give some historical background as to how we got to this point. The year is 1944, and America is about to win this war against Japan and Germany. They organize the Bretton Woods conference in New Hampshire, and the idea is to establish the US dollar as a world reserve currency.

The logic of this is very simple. In World War II, America had to build a lot of factories to supply armaments for its war machine. Now that the war is coming to an end, what do you do with these factories? The answer is you turn these factories from manufacturing munitions and weapons to manufacturing TVs, cars for the global market.

The problem is the entire world is destroyed because of World War II. What America did was lend the world the money in order to buy cars and washing machines and television sets. This became the basis for Pax Americana as well as the US dollar system.

Because America was lending so much money to Europe and to Japan, it needed collateral for this financing, and this collateral, of course, was gold. The agreement was that US dollars would always be pegged to gold. We call this a gold standard, and it worked great for the first 10, 20 years because it allowed the average American middle-class person to live like a Roman emperor.

If you were a white male in the 1950s, you were in paradise. You had maybe a factory job, but with that factory job, you could have your wife work at home. You could raise three kids and have them all go to college. You could go on vacation twice a year. You had two cars. It really was the best life.

Unfortunately, America started to waste a lot of this, what we call exorbitant privilege, the right to print US dollars. America started to do stupid things, like, for example, the war in Vietnam, the space race, the Great Society. At this point, the world recognized that maybe America is spending too much money.

At the same time, the rest of the world is catching up to America industrially. Germany and Japan were devastated in the war, but they're working really hard, and now their industrial capacity is surpassing that of the United States. What's happened is America went from a creditor nation to a debtor nation. That's bad because you owe everyone gold, and there's not enough gold in the world to pay off the debt.

What happens is in 1971, Richard Nixon declares, “Remember how in 1944 we agreed that US dollars would be pegged to gold? The gold standard? Well, forget about it. From now on, the US dollar, it's all free-floating. It's just fiat currency. We will not give you gold for US dollars.”

Now this creates a crisis of confidence, and to resolve this crisis of confidence, Nixon does two things. He visits Saudi Arabia and agrees to get them to sell oil only in US dollars. We call this the petrodollar. The other thing that he does is he goes to China and gets China to start to liberalize its economy, to start working in the United States. Basically, what China does is use its cheap labor in order to manufacture goods for the global economy and sell its cheap labor in US dollars.

These two things, what happened in the Middle East and what happened in East Asia, now become the new framework for the global economy. The idea is that the Middle East will sell its oil to East Asia so that Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China could then make manufactured goods to sell the world. All this is being facilitated in US dollars. All this money, because it's being facilitated in US dollars, goes back to America.

Because of this global system, America now has to shift from a manufacturing power to a financial power in order to process all this trade. This has led to the financialization, the hollowing out of the American manufacturing sector. This has led to tremendous problems in American society.

For one thing, it's led to tremendous inequality. Another thing is that America now is forced to provide security guarantees for the entire world, so its military is overextended. This is what is called imperial overstretch. Another thing that happens is there's so much power in the financial sector that it leads to corruption.

This is what obviously led to the 2008 subprime crisis because you got these Wall Street banks out of control, and they were all engaged in speculation. They didn't really care because they knew that, no matter what happened, the government would pick up the tab at the end of the day. They engaged in all this reckless behavior, and this has led to the world that we live in today.

Obama was elected in 2008 to fix these issues, to represent the working class. But he didn't do that. That's why in 2016 we got Donald Trump, who promised to build a wall to stop illegal immigration. He also promised to basically prevent the world from taking advantage of America. This has led to the Trump years.

## The causes of imperial decline

### Is this preordained or a series of political accidents?

Answer:

I would say we are in an age of imperial decline. If you look at history, empires decline for very much the same reasons, and the pattern of decline is very similar. I will say there are three major causes of American imperial decline.

The first is financialization. Thomas Piketty talks about this in his book Capital in the Twenty-First Century , where, as capitalism progresses, eventually you reach a point where it's much more lucrative to do financial speculation than it is to do real wealth creation.

Let's just imagine you're an entrepreneur, and you work really hard, like Ally, and you create a lot of wealth. You hire a lot of people, and now you have a lot of savings. What you do with these savings is you invest in other enterprises. You engage in financial speculation, and what you realize is, “Wow, financial speculation is a lot more profitable than real wealth creation, like opening a business.”

This is just how capitalism works. Thomas shows that, over time, just the logic of capitalism, because it is really the consolidation of capital in the hands of really smart investors, then stock market speculation will be a lot more lucrative than real wealth creation.

The example he gives is, on average, if you put your money in the stock market, you might get 5% returns. If you open a restaurant or open a factory, you might get a 2% return a year. Eventually, you reach a point where, “I'm not going to go open a restaurant or start a business. I'll just spend my money in the stock market.” That's where we are today. It's much more lucrative to go play the stock market or cryptocurrency than it is to open a factory. That's number one.

Number two is you also have the bureaucratization of society, meaning that these bureaucracies that were meant to coordinate and centralize resources become bigger and bigger over time until they become parasites.

The classic example is our universities. If you go to a university in the 1950s, it was really about making sure the professors could teach well and do research. ### How do you retain so much information?

## Three models of the nation state

First, what many of you will ask: well, what then is a nation state? Well, historically, we've had three major examples of nation states. And they're all different examples. Let's start with France. If you know your history, France has something called a social contract. We choose to surrender our freedom in order to work in society, in order to create a society. But in return for our freedom, we must be given rights.

And this creates the idea of the citizen. And even today, if you go to France, I'm not sure if any of you have lived in France, but they take this idea of citizenship very very seriously. And it's created a lot of conflict in France because there are many Muslims who want to wear the hijab and the French are like, "No, we are a secular nation state with a social contract. We don't allow that. We're not religious."

But what made the social contract possible was not a piece of paper. It was through blood. Specifically the French Revolution, right? And the Napoleonic Wars. That's what established France as a nation state, the sacrifice of the people in return for eternal and inalienable rights guaranteed by the state. That's the French model, a social contract brought about by a people's revolution. And it's still in effect today. And as I said, the French are very proud of this achievement. Then you have Germany.

For Germany, it's iron and blood. It is the language. It is theritage, the culture that makes you German. And this is interesting. # Emergency Discussion #3: Xi Visits Trump

## The summit and the state dinner

This is only the second of four meetings that are scheduled between Trump and Xi this year. Trump first visited China in May, and that went well but didn't really produce anything. This visit went okay, but again it didn't produce anything. There are two more visits scheduled. One will be at APEC in China, in Shenzhen, in November, and Putin is scheduled to be there as well. President Xi has invited Trump to China, and Trump has said yes. I think it's very likely all three leaders will be there for the first time in a long time: Putin of Russia, Xi of China, and Trump of the United States. That'll be very interesting. In December, there will be one more meeting in Florida, at Trump's National Golf Course, and President Xi will probably be there for the G20 summit.

Before the meeting, there was a meeting between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his counterpart, He Lifeng , in New York at the JPMorgan offices, and they were trying to figure out a trade deal. As you know, there is a pause to the trade war between the United States and China, and they basically extended it by a few months. It didn't seem as though there were some major results out of these meetings. They were supposed to discuss the possibility of establishing an AI committee, a global committee, to discuss guardrails and all that. I don't think that happened either. These meetings are happening, but for whatever reason they are extremely lackluster.

You can make the argument, and it's a very legitimate argument, that right now U.S.–China relations are under tremendous strain. Remember, there is another U.S. citizen—I forgot his name—but he was in South China doing some research, and he was apprehended by the Chinese authorities and detained and arrested on the suspicion of spying. That has caused a lot of tension between China and the United States. Also, the United States has accused China of providing targeting information for the Iranians, which has allowed the Iranians to kill Americans. There's a lot of conflict between China and the United States.

My intuition is that a lot of this isn't really conflict between the United States and China. A lot of it is different factions within both the United States and within China who are trying to railroad each other, who are trying to embarrass each other's factions. Right now, in the United States, there are certain factions that want rapprochement with China. There are also many different factions that want to increase belligerence, to increase this conflict between China and the United States, and that's what's really driving a lot of these news leaks.

Something to note is how President Trump went directly to Joint Base Andrews to greet President Xi. This was a very big deal. The last time this happened was when Obama went and greeted the Pope. This is Trump showing the greatest hospitality to President Xi. There was also a flyover, and the two first ladies also spent a lot of time together. There was this big state dinner, and this is only the second state dinner that Trump has hosted in his second term. The first was for King Charles. Clearly, the emphasis is purely on business. That's point number one.

Point number two is, as you can see from this list, most of these people happen to work in the AI, high-tech sector, and that really highlights Trump's priority. Larry Fink and Stephen Schwarzman are heavy, heavy investors in AI databases, especially Larry Fink. That's what Trump wants. He's a business person, right? China has been very, very reluctant to do so. I don't think it's because China is trying to protect its own sovereignty. I think it's because no one is in charge of China right now. No one person has the authority to make any controversial concessions.

I know this is a very provocative statement, but let me slowly explain to you my logic. My argument to you today is that in China, there's really no one in charge. It's rule by committee .

## Three paradoxes and three misunderstandings

There are three paradoxes that I saw during this summit. The big paradox is there were no Chinese entrepreneurs present. Why this is important is it violates two important Chinese principles: the principle of reciprocity and equality. If you come to my house and I invite these Chinese entrepreneurs, then when I go to your house, it's expected that I bring Chinese entrepreneurs as well. This is the idea of reciprocity. It's like giving gifts. If I give you a nice gift, you have to give me a nice gift back in return.

It also violates the principle of equality. China sees itself as a peer to the United States. The question then is, why is it that all these American titans of industry were present, but these Chinese titans of industry were not present? Does that mean to say that China does not have any titans? Does it mean to say that the Chinese economy is not important? It's a really weird thing. Remember, in China these things happen for political purposes. Clearly, things were arranged in order to deliver a certain political message to the Chinese people. What we're trying to figure out is, what is this message? That's the first paradox.

The second paradox is there was a rumor this year, in May, that China would invest $1 trillion in the United States, primarily setting up these EV factories. China has these EV cars that are very popular, very cheap, and they dominate the global market. There was this rumor that China would announce a trillion dollars in investment in the United States. It may still happen. Remember, there's still three months to go before the year ends, and they might save it for the G20. It may still happen, but it has not happened yet.

This is very strange because usually, when you are a Chinese president and you come to the United States, you want to show how powerful you are by offering a major gift. The only thing that President Xi has offered so far is two pandas. That's kind of strange.

The third paradox is there have been no major announcements during this summit. In fact, you can argue that things have regressed since the May summit. Usually, they would want to create a narrative where things are progressing, but it seems as though there are these major setbacks this time around.

This is what Donald Trump said on Truth Social :

Very productive meeting with President Xi for both the U.S.A. and China. Tremendous things will be happening. Like almost everyone else, he seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE.
