Again, usually a Chinese president, when he visits the United States, tries to offer a gesture of goodwill. The gesture of goodwill is he wants to invite 100,000 young Americans to study in China over the next five years. Sure. Elon Musk telegraphed this a few days before the actual announcement in his interview with China Media Group , which says that they are in coordination.

To understand what's going on, you need to understand three things about China. I know this is going to be hard. Once you accept these three things, then everything starts to make more sense. When you read, when you consume media—New York Times, BBC, CNN—you are misled into believing certain things. I think that's why the expectations were so high for the summit. But living in China, knowing China very well—in fact, I know China better than any other country in the world—I will say there are three major misunderstandings about China.

The first, and what people don't appreciate, is the Chinese economy is in decline. It peaked back in 2014, 2015, and now it is in steady decline. That's point one.

Point two is Xi Jinping is not really in charge of China. I know this is going to shock everyone, but he's not in charge. If he were really in charge, if anyone were in charge, China would not be behaving the way it's behaving. China has been extremely passive these past two years. It's done really nothing, and this is while the world is burning. China has been extremely quiet and passive. A lot of people are saying, well, this is just China's strategic, long-term, patient thinking. That's not true. It's because no one's in charge. That's the real reason.

This gets to my third point, which is China is not able to think strategically because no one's in charge. It can only respond to crises, like the U.S. invasion or the U.S. attack on Iran. That's my central, central argument to you today.

## Chinese entrepreneurs and technology companies

Let's get to the first question, which is why no Chinese entrepreneurs showed up at the state banquet. A lot of the reason why is Chinese entrepreneurs have been under a lot of pressure lately. It started two, three years ago with Jack Ma falling from grace. But now it's even extended to Ren Zhengfei, who is the founder of Huawei.

If you know China, you know that Huawei is a Chinese military company, and it is probably the most powerful company in China right now. It receives billions, possibly hundreds of billions of dollars, in state subsidies, mainly to create its own semiconductor ecosystem. For the past couple of weeks, both Ren Zhengfei, the founder of Huawei, and his daughter, Meng Wanzhou, have disappeared. It is impossible for people to get in touch with them, including the executives who work under them. This is extremely, extremely unusual.

Huawei is a public company, and it has a massive PR operation in order to squash any rumors, and it has not done so. This is extremely unusual. There are rumors that he has fled the country. I don't know where he would go to, but there are rumors that he's fled the country. There are rumors that he is under investigation.

Why would he be under investigation? Huawei has been promoting the fact that it's developed its own semiconductors that are high-tech, and it's been able to circumvent the U.S.-dominant global supply chain. It doesn't need photolithography machines from ASML. It doesn't need to buy chips from Nvidia. The rumor is, it turns out that this is all BS. It turns out that whatever innovations Huawei has made in these past few years, it's because they've smuggled in Nvidia chips through other sources.

Quite honestly, living in China, being Chinese, knowing China very well, I would say it is far more plausible that Huawei was smuggling in chips than Huawei developed its own innovative semiconductors. Just being Chinese and knowing how China works, Chinese are much more likely to cheat than to innovate.

Regardless, I think the Huawei first family is in a lot of trouble, and the reason why they haven't announced this yet is it's completely embarrassing. It's entirely possible that Ren Zhengfei will return and everyone will pretend nothing happened. The reason why is it would be too embarrassing for China to admit that Huawei was lying to everyone all along. But as you can see, because of this issue, the Chinese would be reluctant to showcase entrepreneurs at the White House because it really doesn't know who it can trust.

Some other news is there are rumors that the Chinese are investigating DeepSeek and Kimi. This is huge because DeepSeek has been a source of tremendous national pride these past few years. Remember what happened was that OpenAI released ChatGPT, and then, using a fraction of the resources, of the time, of the personnel of OpenAI, DeepSeek was able to create a much more efficient large language model than OpenAI. Again, this was a source of tremendous pride.

DeepSeek said that was because they created more efficient algorithms that were able to parse the internet much faster than OpenAI. It seems like that's not what happened. It seems what happened was that DeepSeek basically created thousands, possibly millions of accounts, and basically mirrored or stole the database of OpenAI and just used it for itself. It's a practice that these Chinese AI companies are continuing to use.

The problem with that is, what's been happening is that Chinese military personnel have been asking AI some really sensitive questions and providing some really sensitive Chinese military intelligence to the AI, and this is going back to the U.S. companies. Basically, these U.S. AI companies are now able to have their own Chinese military database, have access to the Chinese military personnel database. As a result, this has compromised Chinese national security interests.

Again, guys, I live in China. Chinese people do not innovate. They just cheat and they steal. This is what happens when we pull this crap. Huawei thought it was being really smart by smuggling these Nvidia chips. But these Nvidia chips probably had some backdoor that allowed the U.S. NSA to create backdoors to access Huawei secrets.

Look, think about this. Just a thought experiment. For years and years, you know that Huawei engineers have been stealing IP left and right from Western companies. There are videos of Huawei engineers going into telecom firms in the United States and then stealing the hardware. There are videos like that. If you know that they're going to do that, and you know that all they're going to do is reverse-engineer what you have, and they don't really know what the source code is, then why aren't you going to create these backdoors?

### Audience comment: BMW and technology transfer

Audience: I have something to support what you're saying about extending the technology. In 2013, I was in BMW Munich, in Germany, and I was having a tour. From Germany, they investigated the fact: why is it happening that we don't have any accidents in Germany, and we have a lot of accidents in China?

It popped up that those employees who were working in that factory, after an eight-hour shift, were going 60 kilometers away, and there was another factory which was exactly the copy-paste of what the Germans did there in China. The reason for that was just to copy the whole concept of the car. That resulted in the management pulling out everything from China and starting to ship the cars back as they were up to 2012. But the technology was lost, and we have a result now that the cars that the Chinese are producing are much better than the cars that we produce in Europe. In a sense, technology is everything, is power-based. Just to support your idea.

### Audience comment: Huawei and semiconductor innovation

Audience: Professor, something I don't agree with you, because I worked in semiconductors for over ten years. In 2010, moving to AI, good connection with Huawei and all these guys. Because the U.S. government said that if you work in Huawei, it's impossible for you to get into the USA. That is the biggest problem.

You should understand that Huawei is facing much more challenges than anybody can see, because the U.S. government uses all their power against one company, Huawei, equipped with all the technology, all the high-tech giants of the USA. It is the fact, and all the chipsets sold in China have the backdoor.

Response: That's absolutely right. The United States is intent on destroying Huawei. The reason why is Huawei has been very successful at penetrating foreign markets, which is a direct threat to U.S. companies such as Intel, Nvidia, and Apple. That's why the U.S. is intent on destroying Huawei and any companies that are trying to penetrate into the global market. If Huawei just stayed in China, then the United States would obviously have no problem with Huawei stealing every American IP.

Audience: Also, in the world, only Huawei can compete with Silicon Valley plus Israel. But in fact, now Silicon Valley doesn't have any advantage of innovation. Why? They don't have the new technology. I totally agree about the AI companies and semiconductor innovation. I work very deeply in Israel. But I only use one of the budget, one of the $1 million U.S., hire engineers in Israel. The Israeli engineer can deliver in high quality and timely. In fact, Israel is the center of semiconductor innovation. Silicon Valley is gone.

Response: It's very true that Silicon Valley has become extremely corrupt, inefficient, and all they're interested in is rent-seeking. They want to control Washington, D.C., and they want to prevent innovation from happening. That's why they are banning these Chinese open AI models. That's exactly correct, and that's exactly the issue facing the United States right now.

Again, the Chinese are having problems with their entrepreneurs. It seems as though these Chinese technologists have not been transparent about what's really going on. In fact, a lot of these Chinese technology companies are cutting corners in order to please state officials. Remember, maybe in the United States these entrepreneurs like Elon Musk have all the power, but in China these entrepreneurs, no matter how wealthy they become, are still servants to the state.

## Exit restrictions and the Chinese economy

Another thing that's been happening, and this is really important, is on September 15, China announced changes to its exit and entry administration . Basically, the thing to remember is now China has the authority to ban any entrepreneurial and technological and scientific talent from leaving the country for no reason whatsoever. They can just say national security, and they can prevent you from leaving the country.

I think this is a response to the fact that there are a lot of wealthy entrepreneurs who are trying to flee the country. It's really interesting what's happened these past 30 years, because from 2000 to 2020, if you were a Silicon Valley engineer who was of Chinese descent, what you would do is take your knowledge and the code that you created, and maybe you would steal some IP as well. You'd fly back to China to create a company, and you'd get a lot of financing and state support in order to do so. You made a lot of money that way.

That's what was happening from 2000 to about 2020: thousands of these Chinese engineers coming back from Silicon Valley and then using their knowledge and know-how to create Chinese versions of American companies. This minted lots of millionaires and billionaires. But now what they want to do is take this money and go to the West because, unlike China, there's respect for private property rights in the Western world. China has been trying very hard to stop this trend, and now it just made the decision: we don't care if you want to leave, but you made a lot of money in this country; we won't let you leave.

This is scaring a lot of very wealthy people. But it just shows you the tumultuous state of the Chinese economy and of the Chinese middle class right now.

This is a new book called Broken China , by Logan Wright. I've actually not read the book, but his central argument is something that I've been arguing my entire time in China, which is that in 2008, after the subprime crisis in the United States, the Chinese leadership freaked out because they were afraid that the global economy would collapse and China would lose its export market. The response of the Chinese government was to invest heavily in infrastructure spending.

This is not because the Chinese think long term, guys. It's not because they have this great grand vision for how to foster innovation in China. They do not. It was a response to the subprime crisis in the United States. This bubble was great for the entrepreneurial elite, but it's led to lots and lots of debt. It led to a lot of corruption. Now we're living in a time when they're trying to unwind this debt, unwind this corruption.

You think, well, the United States has $40 trillion in debt. That's really bad. Actually, the Chinese debt situation is much, much worse than the United States, and people don't appreciate this. If you don't believe me, then I suggest picking up this book, Broken China , by Logan Wright. I'm not going to read it because this is the system I've known for a long, long time. People are now slowly waking up to the fact that the Chinese are not these brilliant Machiavellian strategists. They're just corrupt as hell. It's that simple, guys. There's no magic here. They're just corrupt.

## The military commission and political struggle

Another thing that has been happening in China that has gotten a lot of international attention is the political struggle within China. This is the highest military body in China. You can say it's really the most powerful body of China: seven people, the military commission which controls the military. There are supposed to be seven members, and after three years of purges, we are now left with two.

There are some who say, well, it just shows the consolidation of power under Xi. Look, if you are a dictator, you don't want this crap to happen. It makes you look really, really bad. It makes you look like a fool. Think about this: if you're a dictator, what happened here? Why is a seven-member commission only staffed by two people?

There are different possibilities. One is you're just stupid, and you appointed people you can't trust, and you had to fire them. In which case, why are you dictator? That's number one. Number two is, well, they were corrupt, and that's what the Chinese media reported. But again, why do you appoint corrupt people to this position?

What this really shows us is the intense political struggles within China, where different factions are trying to knock off different people. Because of the intense political struggle, China is in stalemate right now. Again, this makes China look really, really bad. There's a seven-member commission. What you should be doing is replacing these people as you go. The fact that this is so open and it's so blatant and so transparent shows you really no one's in charge, and it's just these different political factions going after each other.

## Mao, the Cultural Revolution, and Deng's consensus

Having gone through that, I want to explain to you a quick history of the People's Republic of China so you understand the context in which all this political struggle is happening. Once you understand the history, I think it's fairly easy to project into the future and see where China is heading.

The year is 1949, and a miracle happens. This guerrilla army that was basically fighting a guerrilla insurgency for the past 20 years is now ruler of China under Mao Zedong . People don't appreciate this. They think of him as this communist ideologue. He was not a communist ideologue. He was first and foremost a messianic figure who believed that he was God's champion, who would help China stand up and be a dominant power in the world.

That's why they ushered in something called the Great Leap Forward. The Great Leap Forward was a plan to, within five years, change China from an agricultural nation into an industrial powerhouse. That basically meant just shifting farmers from the fields to the factories. If you know any Chinese history, you will know that this was a disaster for China. It led to a great famine where millions of people perished.

The reason why is they focused so much on industrial production that they forgot to grow food. Because at this time China was an autarky, meaning it didn't really trade with the rest of the world, China refused to ask for help from the rest of the world. Rather than just say to the world, socialism doesn't really work, guys, and we need to buy some food from you, they'd rather just let their people starve.

Eventually, the famine caused by the Great Leap Forward would lead to something called the Cultural Revolution , which happened between 1966 and 1976. What people don't appreciate about the Cultural Revolution is it happened in different phases.

Because of the Great Leap Forward, Mao's leadership was challenged by the rest of the Communist Party. The Communist Party elite got together and said, listen, Mao, you were a great leader, but maybe you're too old, and maybe it's time to transfer power to younger technocrats who know how to manage the affairs of the state. Mao Zedong went along with this for a few years, but then he decided, I'm the messiah, people follow me, and these technocrats will just turn China into a corrupt oligarchy, which was the case for thousands of years. Why did we fight the revolution?

Mao Zedong promoted the Cultural Revolution, where he encouraged the people to rise up against the bureaucrats, against the bureaucratic elite, and overthrow them. For about two, three years, there were these massive purges of the bureaucratic elite. But then Mao was like, these kids, these teenagers, the Red Guards, are kind of out of control. He called in the military to purge these revolutionaries. That was the second phase of the Cultural Revolution.

Now the military is in charge, and Mao Zedong appointed a successor called Lin Biao, who was basically head of the military. But then they had a falling-out, and Lin Biao tried to escape to Russia, and he was killed when his plane crashed. That created the third phase of the Cultural Revolution, which is basically China became a theocracy under Mao Zedong, and it remained so until 1976, when Mao died.

When Mao died, he appointed a successor who would continue his legacy. But the Chinese bureaucratic elite, the communist old guard, got together and said, no, we don't want any more of this crap. We want to restore our own power base. Under Deng Xiaoping, they came back.

What's really important for us to appreciate is, from the perspective of the communist old guard, the worst thing that happened to China was not capitalism. It was not the Sino-Soviet split. It was Mao's messianism. They were afraid of two things. One, they were really afraid that a dictator would arise and basically restore Mao's legacy. They were afraid of Maoism. They were also really afraid of people's religious tendencies, because the Cultural Revolution was a theocracy. They were really afraid of the power of religion.

Under Deng Xiaoping, they created all sorts of policies in order to ensure that these two things, Maoism and messianism, would never, ever arise in China. To facilitate this process, Deng Xiaoping visited the United States. This is Deng Xiaoping in Texas putting on a ten-gallon hat .

This was, of course, a diplomatic breakthrough because it endeared the American population to this old communist zealot. This allowed for China and the United States to eventually establish a very strong trading relationship, which became the basis for modern-day globalization. But the key for us to remember is that under Deng Xiaoping, they created policies to move away from both Maoism and messianism, and they had certain rules that they all obeyed.

The party elite, the revolutionary vanguard and their children, are untouchable. The princelings are not touchable. You can go after other political opponents, but you cannot go after the families of the red nobility. The red nobility would share in the spoils. They would split up China and divvy up the spoils, and they would not go after each other like they did during the Cultural Revolution. They would maintain unity.

Never again will one person be allowed to have all the power in China. It will be consensus. It will be committee decision-making. It'll be a very technocratic process.

From now on, the focus will be on economics.

The military will stay out of political affairs. This is really important. There'll be a clear demarcation between the military and politics. The military will enjoy the spoils of economic reform, to keep them happy, but they will not engage in political affairs.

All four rules are important for us to remember. Why? Because they've broken all four rules today. This is why it's led to this political stalemate that we have in China. To summarize the four rules: number one, red nobility is untouchable. Rule number two, there will never again be a supreme leader like Mao Zedong. Rule number three, just focus on economics, and that's good. Number four, the military must stay out of political affairs. I'll show you that what's happened under Xi Jinping is they've broken all four rules, and that's why China today is a dumpster fire.

Deng did usher in a time of a new consensus, but there were certain people who felt left out. This was the intellectual class, the university students. The military, the red nobility, benefited from all of those reforms, but the intellectual class felt they wanted to get involved as well. That's what led to the Tiananmen Square protests, and that's what also led to the crackdown. Of course, this really damaged China's international standing.

When Deng died and Jiang Zemin came to power, they were intent on institutionalizing all four of these major consensuses. Under Jiang Zemin, they started this process, but what would happen is that Hu Jintao would then cement this process. One major result of this process is massive spending on infrastructure .

A lot of people are like, well, this just shows you how farsighted China is. The problem is China didn't have the money to spend on this infrastructure.

Why they spent money on this infrastructure, again, was a response to a crisis, which is the 2008 great financial crisis in the United States. Remember, at this time in history, China's main driver of economic reform was its export industry. But once it recognized that the rest of the world could go bankrupt and renege on trade promises, China realized it needed to spend more money on infrastructure.

The best way to understand this infrastructure spending is it was not about building a modern nation. It was about trying to appease as many different political factions as possible within China, and the best way to do that is to bribe everyone. That's how Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao were able to basically calm things down while global markets were in turmoil: let these local elites, let these bankers, these real estate developers, these government officials steal together from the nation, and then China will be very peaceful and stable. For the longest time, it worked, until Xi Jinping came into power.

The problem with Xi Jinping is he is not of the technocratic mold. He didn't rise in the technocracy the way that Jiang Zemin, Zhu Rongji, and Hu Jintao did. He rose as part of the red nobility. His father is considered one of the Eight Immortals, one of the eight families that rule China. As part of Deng Xiaoping's basically divvying up all the spoils, they got Shenzhen. As you know, Shenzhen is one of the wealthiest parts of China today.

When Xi Jinping rose to power, he was considered a compromise candidate. The red nobility and the technocratic elite all saw him as the least likely to rock the boat. Now we can understand how ironic that is today. Back in 2012, 2013, when they anointed him, he was considered the most stable, the least likely to rock the boat, the most consensus candidate. The reason why is his opponent was Bo Xilai .

You had two candidates. You had Xi Jinping; you had Bo Xilai. Bo Xilai was charismatic. He was ambitious, and he was a proven leader. When he was mayor of Dalian, Dalian was one of the fastest-growing cities in China. Then he went over to Chongqing, and he basically promoted Cultural Revolution policies. He got a lot of state subsidies for Chongqing. He went after the mafia. A lot of Chinese people thought, this is a great leader. But a lot of Chinese leaders were like, oh my God, if he comes to power, he'll probably end up like Mao Zedong.

Of these two—Xi Jinping, who at that time had absolutely no major accomplishments, and Bo Xilai, a very charismatic, ambitious person—you always pick the other guy. You pick the guy who is less likely to rock the boat. But then what happened is a series of events that no one really expected, which allowed Xi Jinping to cement power in a way that was unprecedented in modern Chinese politics. Remember, Deng Xiaoping created all these institutional systems to ensure no one like Mao Zedong would arise again, and then slowly Xi Jinping broke down all these systems.

The first thing that happened is that after the party elders, after the Chinese picked Xi Jinping to be leader, Bo Xilai staged a coup. He tried to wrestle power from Xi Jinping.

### Was Tiananmen Square a democracy protest or a color revolution?

Audience: Can you comment on Tiananmen Square? Do you think it was a genuine democracy protest or a CIA color revolution thing?

Response: What I said was Tiananmen Square was a response by the intellectual class to what they felt was being left behind by these reforms. The reforms that the party was instituting benefited primarily the military as well as the red nobility, and the intellectual class felt that they were being left behind.

One thing that they really protested, one demand that they had, was at this time China was still a socialist country. You went to a university in China, and you graduated. They sent you off to a faraway place in the middle of nowhere to work as a bureaucrat, and you were like, screw that, I want to be in Beijing or Shanghai. I wouldn't say it was a color revolution. I wouldn't even say it was a democracy protest. It was really about a privileged group in society, university students, who wanted more power and more rights. Honestly, after Tiananmen Square, they got everything that they wanted. That's what I think happened.

## How Xi consolidated power

Back to Bo Xilai. He stages his coup d'état, and so the party leadership had no choice but to rally around Xi Jinping and give him more power in order to stamp out the threat of Bo Xilai. Remember, under Deng Xiaoping, different families controlled different regions in China. This one guy could possibly summon an army of millions. The only way to stamp out this threat was for everyone to unify under Xi Jinping.

But there's a rule: the red nobility is not touchable. He can't actually kill this guy. He's now under house arrest, even though he did try to launch a coup d'état against the Communist Party. That's one major event that helped to solidify and consolidate Xi's power.

Another major event was the trade war, because after Donald Trump and Xi Jinping met , Donald Trump basically launched a trade war against China. That really helped to solidify Xi's power, because previously a lot of the power was centered in the entrepreneurial middle class. But because they were under threat from this trade war, that allowed the political system to consolidate more power. That's number two.

Number three, of course, and the most important, is COVID. I was in China during COVID, and when COVID first happened, I was like, this will last maybe two days and it'll go away. I know this because in 2003 I also experienced SARS. What happened was that during SARS, there was no government mandate. There was no government order. People just decided to lock themselves in apartments for two weeks, and then SARS went away.

That's how diseases work. That's how these viruses work. There have to be these infection points, contagion points, for it to spread. If people are just in their apartments, then this thing goes away really quickly. If you know about viruses, you know their malicious nature, their malignity, decreases over time. But instead, China chose to lock down the country for four years, which is really weird. Why that happened is it allowed Xi Jinping to consolidate power onto himself. He created this huge bureaucracy around him in order to deal with COVID.

Now, to be fair, what I do know is when the virus first broke out in Wuhan, it was a bioweapon. It was killing a lot of people. The reporting back then was that when you first got the virus in Wuhan, your lungs burned. They're like a furnace. It was a real serious threat, and that's what gave Xi the authority to lock down the entire country for four years and create this really absurd authoritarian regime.

Look, look, look. This is a picture of guys getting swabs .

If you're a medical professional, you know for a fact these swab tests are not very accurate. Don't tell me that just by swabbing your mouth, I'm able to diagnose effectively whether or not you have COVID. It was all just theater. But if you got unlucky, if you tested positive, you were sent to the detention center for a month. This is worse than the Cultural Revolution. Why they did this was it allowed Xi Jinping to consolidate power under himself.

The other thing that he did that was really important was he collapsed the real estate bubble. To be fair, a lot of things he did I actually agree with, because remember I said that during the Hu Jintao–Wen Jiabao period, it was just blatant corruption, and it was just too much debt. He inherited this mess, and he had to take certain steps in order to address these issues, or they would just blow up.

I agree with what he did in the real estate market, which is he basically caused the real estate bubble to collapse by refusing to bail out companies that were in default. Evergrande was the classic example, where it was basically a Ponzi scheme, and they thought they were too big to fail. They could always secure funding from the local government. Xi put an end to that, and that has caused this cascading effect, this chain reaction where China's real estate market has collapsed. Again, I think this is a very positive thing because the real estate market was completely unsustainable. But that's also allowed him to consolidate power.

These are things that he was not really in control of, but there are things that were happening, and it was clear that he might have had some part in them. Remember how I said in the 1980s, basically the bureaucratic elite got together and said, we agree not to kill each other the way that we were killing each other during the Cultural Revolution. We agree to play by certain rules and conventions. We agree to play nice. Xi Jinping broke all these rules.

One example is Ling Jihua. Ling Jihua is actually the secretary to President Hu Jintao. If you know anything about the Chinese system, you know that these people are extremely powerful people because they are the gatekeepers. If you want to meet Hu Jintao, you have to go through this guy. Also, he's basically Hu Jintao's bagman. If you want to bribe Hu Jintao for anything, you have to bribe this guy.

Early on in Xi Jinping's tenure, Ling Jihua's son died in a Ferrari car crash , and it was pretty morbid. The details have not been confirmed, but there were rumors that the guy was naked with two other girls, and they were both drunk when they had this horrific car crash. Because of this horrific car crash, there's a massive investigation into Ling Jihua, the father—Ling Gu is the son—and they found out, of course, he was corrupt. They jailed him, and this did a lot in destroying Hu Jintao's power base.

There are rumors that this is a complete setup, that basically some secret police created a situation in order to implicate the father. Ling Jihua himself believes that his son is innocent, and his son was basically murdered in order to frame him. But this event—and again, I can't confirm the veracity of what happened; the Chinese authorities say it was an accident; I can't say it was an accident or not—did weaken Hu Jintao's power base and allow Xi to further consolidate power.

Another thing is the New York Times got hold of Wen Jiabao's financial records , which is, by the way, impossible to do. I actually know the reporter who broke the story. In 2012, there was a New York Times reporter, David Barboza, who broke the story of the Wen Jiabao family's corruption. To break the story, he went through thousands and thousands of SEC filings.

Honestly, maybe if you had a staff of 10,000, you had 10,000 years, you could pull this off. He was able to pull this off in a matter of days, which tells me someone was feeding him this information. Yes, I understand you did go through the filings, and yes, you did prove that these companies tie back to the Wen family. I understand that. But someone had to point you in the right direction. It was like trying to find a needle in a haystack. Someone had to tell you exactly where to look for you to find that.

We can speculate as to who might have pointed this reporter for the New York Times in the right direction. We can also say, because of the scandal, Wen Jiabao's power base was severely depleted. That allowed Xi to further consolidate power. Again, you're not supposed to do this crap. There's a consensus where the top leadership would not engage in these political struggles against each other, because they did this during the Cultural Revolution. They know exactly what happened during the Cultural Revolution. You can see Deng Xiaoping's consensus breaking down.

You would also have these really silly leaks where somehow U.S. intelligence got news that the Chinese army had missiles filled with water instead of fuel .

The big thing is, in 2022, Xi Jinping was able to get a third term. The constitution says that a president should only be in power for two terms. He broke that convention established by Deng Xiaoping and his people, and he got a third term. The peak of his power was getting a third term, but also having Hu Jintao escorted out of the Great Hall of the People .

There's a lot of speculation as to what happened, why Hu Jintao was escorted out. The thing to remember is whenever something is televised in China, it's a highly choreographed event. They spend days with a thousand people figuring out the camera angle, the lighting, the clothes that the leaders wear, how the leaders are depicted. They spend a lot of time on this. Each of these guys, even a provincial leader, will have thousands in a PR office just going, combing over how this person is portrayed on the internet and in the media. This is really important for these people.

The idea, well, Hu Jintao shouldn't have been there, and they had to remove him because he got lost somewhere—that's absurd. This is a highly choreographed event meant to embarrass Hu Jintao, to show that Xi Jinping was in the ascendancy. In 2022, basically the consensus that Deng Xiaoping had established was now completely broken, and now you have one man in charge.

The problem is, and this is really important for you guys to remember, China is much too big for one person to control. Also, Mao was a messiah who proved himself the messiah by obtaining power through the will of God. This guy inherited his throne. Because he saw himself as Mao, basically all these different political factions decided they needed to get rid of this guy. The best way to do that is you destroy the people who he put into power.

In China, personnel is politics, politics is personnel . The way you basically struggle against each other for power is by going after each person's associates.

## Purges, foreign trips, and Xi's position

The first person to fall was Foreign Minister Qin Gang . This is a huge scandal in China, where Qin Gang was personally appointed by President Xi Jinping, and then news got out that he had a concubine who decided to have a child in the United States. This child was a U.S. citizen. The child's father was Qin Gang. This got out. We can speculate as to how they got the news. I would imagine that they got the news from the Americans.

One thing to appreciate is these U.S. spies work very, very closely with these Chinese spies because ultimately what they're interested in are these domestic political struggles as opposed to these international political struggles. He was forced to resign. Then the defense minister, very shortly, was forced to resign because of corruption. Again, people struggle as to how this happened. Then you have two generals who are forced to resign because of corruption.

All these rules that Deng had established in the 1980s to ensure that Maoism would never arise again—number one, never allow someone to consolidate all power; number two, don't allow the military to engage in politics; number three, make sure everything is consensus; number four, focus on the economy—it's all being destroyed now. The military is now forced into all this political factionalism, which is destroying the military's capacity to maintain order. In fact, you can now argue the military is a source of a lot of disorder in China today.

You have, again, seven members in this military commission , and now you only have two. Everyone else has been replaced. The most important has been Zhang Youxia. Zhang Youxia was considered the military equivalent to Xi Jinping. Xi Jinping was in control of politics, but Zhang Youxia was in control of the gun. Again, remember, in the Chinese system these two forces are meant to be parallel with each other. In theory, the politics controls the gun, but in reality they're supposed to be equal.

Zhang Youxia's father is also another major general, so he has the pedigree, the credibility to counter Xi Jinping. There's a lot of rumors, there's a lot of speculation that Zhang Youxia was behind a lot of the purges against Xi Jinping's people, and Zhang Youxia was trying to constrain Xi Jinping's power. But because Xi Jinping is the president, and they didn't want things to blow out of control, they agreed to let him stay in power.

In response, Xi Jinping decided that he would basically cross the Rubicon, and he ordered the arrest of Zhang Youxia. There are rumors that actually Zhang Youxia is dead, but in January this year, Zhang Youxia was arrested, and a couple of weeks ago he was expelled by the party for factionalism, for engaging in factionalism.

China right now, it's just a dumpster fire. No one's in control, and they're all trying to destroy each other, which basically means that Xi Jinping himself has absolutely no power.

One thing that is really strange is this is the list of his foreign trips in 2023 , and as you can see, it's really not that much. He doesn't really go out that much. In 2025 , look at all these countries: Vietnam, Malaysia, Cambodia, Russia, Kazakhstan, South Korea. The thing that distinguishes these places is they're really close to China. This guy, when he leaves, he doesn't go that far. The reason why is because of so much political struggle within the country, you need to make sure that you're around to make sure the different factions don't conspire against you.

This is even more blatant in 2026 , where for the first half of the year he really didn't go out. But then we see, for whatever reason, August, September, he's going to a lot of places, and we can speculate as to why. Again, we can only speculate because the Chinese system is a political black box. We can speculate that he's consolidated power, and so he's invincible, and so he can do whatever he wants. That's one possibility.

Another possibility is he's stripped of all power because his personnel, the people loyal to him, have been stripped of their power, and so he's a lame president. Next year he'll be replaced, and his job is now to go out and represent China. One piece of evidence to support this is he does not look healthy. If you're a supreme dictator, you tend to have a certain confidence to you. You have a certain swagger to you.

This is in 2023, when he's visiting San Francisco . By 2023, he looks pretty tired. He does not look like a supreme leader. Compare him to Putin or Modi or Trump, really.

I want to show you guys another video . This is two days ago, when Xi came to the United States. Look at the way he holds on to his wife's hand, and look at the way he is walking down the stairs. He does not look healthy.

## U.S.–China relations, resources, and financial markets

### What would happen if Canada's potash supply were disrupted?

Audience: I also noticed the same thing you did about how he had to hold Peng's hand as he walked down the airplane steps. Then, when he was on the ground, he also seemed kind of nervous or agitated. Xi kept having to look left and right. I don't know what he was trying to see, but he looked surprisingly nervous. The expressions of the other security members and the Chinese governors who were with him also seemed to have different reactions when they were meeting with President Trump. Xi just seemed kind of normal, but the other people were excited, and then some of the people seemed indifferent. It just seems very scattered.

The actual thing I wanted to focus on is something I think you skipped over in Canada, but I think someone mentioned it during a question, about potash fertilizer, which is potassium fertilizer, which is mined from Canada. A big portion of the world global supply of potash fertilizer, some of it is mined in Canada, and the other two countries you get it from are Belarus and Russia.

For fertilizer, you basically don't have a good substitute for potash fertilizer. You can try to burn wood ash and try to reactivate it with salt or whatever, but you need a ton of industrial processes that you can't set up immediately. In the situation that the United States does attempt some sort of invasion of Canada and that potash fertilizer supply trade is disrupted, what would happen, or what would China try to do about that?

Response: Look, there will be no U.S. invasion of Canada. It's not going to happen. I know that Mark Carney has been talking about it. I know that Mark Carney is like, well, we'll just do guerrilla warfare, and we're ready for the U.S. It's just politics. It's just optics. There's no way the United States will actually launch a ground invasion of Canada.

Look at what happened in Greenland, where for a few months Trump was talking about invading Greenland, but ultimately they signed a deal where the United States has this access to Greenland. Basically, it's just Denmark recognizing that the United States is too powerful militarily, and there's actually no point in trying to resist, so let's just save face and sign a treaty. I think the same thing will happen in Canada.

You're absolutely right, Baron, in that what Trump really wants is control over Canadian resources. Why he wants that is to be able to pressure China into making lots and lots of trade concessions, and fertilizer is a very important part of that. I think this thing will resolve itself naturally, where the Chinese are extremely pragmatic, the Canadian people are extremely pragmatic, and Trump is a business person, and they'll come to an agreement at some point.

But the bigger issue is not fertilizer. You can always access fertilizer. The problem is just a breakdown in global supply chains. We have absolutely no idea how consequential things will be if you break down global supply chains. It's not just that fertilizers are part of the global supply chain. Everything is part of the global supply chain. We haven't really gamed out or war-gamed out what a breakdown in global supply chains looks like. No one's done it. The reason why is it is horrifying to even contemplate the possibility that global trade stops.

Audience: I was later going to ask about soybeans and corn being used for animal feed.

Response: It's the same thing, where China is getting a lot of beans from Brazil right now, and Trump will eventually pressure Brazil into signing a Western Hemisphere trade pact. China's not negotiating with these countries individually, but negotiating with all these countries via the United States. That's what Trump really wants.

### What is the macro impact of the U.S.–China relationship?

Audience: What is the macro impact of this U.S.–China relationship? As you have said, the world is moving towards a multipolar world, so China and the U.S. cannot be a dual-polar power. Is this just a vain effort to try to save the supply chain and economy, which will eventually collapse?

Response: Really, China and the United States are the two main beneficiaries of globalization, and so both are status quo powers. Both are stuck working together to try to save the global economy in a time of war. Unfortunately, I don't think either really wants to do this. They're kind of stuck doing it. They don't have a choice in the matter. If they don't do it, then they'll suffer even more. They're reluctant partners, basically.

Audience: What is the role of tech oligarchs like Elon Musk as an actor in the game? What is the incentive they're working towards, specifically to collaborate with China?

Response: They just want to get more money for themselves. They want access to the China market. They want more subsidies from the Chinese government. For example, you guys may know about China and the United States collaborating together on an AI governance board, to prevent AI from killing humanity. What this really is, it's an attempt on the part of oligarchs, these tech companies, to get money from the government. How do you ensure these tech companies don't go out of control? You nationalize them. When you nationalize them, what happens is these tech oligarchs privatize the gains and socialize the losses. We're living in a time when everyone's trying to steal as much as possible.

### What role do randomness and coincidence play?

Audience: Something I've noticed in your thinking is you seem reluctant to attribute major outcomes to randomness or coincidence. What makes you lean towards a purposeful explanation rather than just accepting that things may be random?

Response: That's a good point. But during my presentation, I did say certain things were random. For example, number one, the COVID thing, I think there's certain randomness to it. I don't think they purposely planned out the lab leak. If they did, I'd be very impressed, but I don't think China actually has the capacity to execute something like that to that extent. I think the COVID lab leak was just an accident. That's random.

I also said that Bo Xilai trying to stage a coup d'état was pretty random as well, and Xi Jinping is just a major beneficiary of these events. But then I also pointed out there are certain things that happened that were probably not random. For example, the car crash. I'm not saying one random event. I'm just saying, if you look at a pattern of things.

### Who is Xi's main opposition?

Audience: Who is the main opposition of Xi? Who is his rival, and do you have any prediction for the 2027 term, supreme leader?

Response: One thing I didn't do was go into the different political factions. Here's the best way to understand it, in a very simple way. China has a lot of provinces. Each of these provinces is controlled by a political clique, and these political cliques can choose to align with each other. That's the best way to understand it.

Basically, President Xi has control over Beijing, and it's in the best interest of these provinces to go along with orders from Beijing in order to project stability. But if things get really bad, then what will happen is these provinces will break away. I think this is something that will happen in the next ten years.

Look at all empires. It's basically these different warlords or these different provincial governors who make the decision it's probably better for them to get along than to fight each other, because fighting each other, there's too much cost. But you always reach a point when, well, we can't settle anything politically, so we're forced to fight things out. I think that China is heading in that direction. The fact that you have only two members of the seven-member military commission still active tells you a lot about how bad things have deteriorated in China.

### Could China buy more U.S. Treasuries in exchange for a Taiwan deal?

Audience: I have a question on the U.S. Treasury holdings from China. I think they went down from $1.2 trillion to right now $600 billion. Do you think there could be a deal between the U.S. and China, to say China has to buy a lot more Treasuries but gets Taiwan in maybe ten years? The yields are really hurting the U.S. economy. What do you think?

Response: This is something that I've been thinking a lot about. Let me explain what's going on. What are U.S. Treasuries? U.S. Treasuries are just debt. Why does China have so much U.S. debt? It's because of the trade imbalance, where the Chinese make a lot of goods and then sell them to the United States, and China doesn't really buy things from the United States. That creates a trade imbalance, and this trade imbalance shows up in U.S. Treasuries, because when you sell things to the United States, they pay you in U.S. dollars. You can take the U.S. dollars and buy U.S. Treasuries.

Basically, another way of saying this is U.S. Treasuries are a way for China to bribe the United States to let China export its goods to the United States. Why would China want this? First of all, it's because China is a plantation economy. It's a slave economy where all that matters is the elite. The people are just energy to be extracted. From the perspective of the elite, this is a great deal, because you're just taking Chinese labor and you are then selling it for U.S. dollars, which they can use to go to the United States and spend money on. That's one real advantage to China.

Another advantage for China is it keeps people busy. It keeps people employed. Even though Chinese workers aren't paid that much, they at least have something to do. It's a lot better than working in the fields. Even though we say it's a slave system, it's still better than the system they had before, which was this feudal system. That's number two.

Number three is, even though U.S. debt, U.S. Treasuries, is not really worth that much, it's still the main basis of the global economy. China can take the U.S. Treasuries and then use them as collateral to go and buy other things, like soybeans from Brazil. The current system for many years benefited both the Chinese elite and the American elite. The people suffered. The U.S. people lost a lot of manufacturing jobs to China. The Chinese people are working for slave wages, but they don't matter.

Why is the system breaking down? The system is breaking down because the United States has proven that it can choose to weaponize its financial system in order to maintain its hegemony. The classic example, of course, is Russia, where Russia has about $300 billion of its assets frozen by Western financial institutions, mainly Europe. Europe froze about $200 billion in Russian assets. Starting then, China's like, uh-oh, what do we do now? What they started to do was basically sell U.S. Treasuries to buy more gold.

We have to remember something. This is really important. It's not one government that controls all these U.S. Treasuries. A lot of these are Chinese corporations who are trying to better hedge risk. Right now there are three major buyers of U.S. Treasuries: Japan, the GCC, and China. Some of you were saying it's the U.K. No, guys, if you live in the U.K., you know the U.K. is not buying U.S. Treasuries because the U.K. has no money. It is the GCC buying U.S. Treasuries with the City of London as the middleman. That's why the U.K. appears number two when it's really the GCC. Number one is Japan, number two is GCC, number three is China.

You're absolutely right in that right now, if these three countries stop buying U.S. Treasuries, then the United States could not finance its debt. Right now it's at $40 trillion. If it's forced to raise interest rates to 5%, 6%, it has to pay $2 trillion a year in interest payments alone. This will create huge problems for the U.S. economy. Therefore, what the United States wants is for Japan, the GCC, and China to continue to buy U.S. Treasuries.

The GCC and Japan aren't a problem because they're essentially U.S. vassals. The United States can force them to buy U.S. weapons. The United States wants the GCC to go to war against the Houthis and the Iranians. The United States wants Japan to go to war against China. China is a much bigger problem because China is independent. It's sovereign. It doesn't need to buy U.S. Treasuries, and you can't actually make China buy U.S. Treasuries.

They're trying to think of a workaround, and the workaround is something called stablecoins. I'm not sure how much you know about stablecoins, but stablecoins are essentially digital currency that is backed by U.S. Treasuries. If China agrees to allow stablecoins into the country, this is a backdoor where Chinese citizens can privately buy U.S. Treasuries through stablecoins. That's the workaround that they want to do.

But the problem is right now there's no one in charge of China. I keep on going back to this point, where no one can make this decision because it's too controversial. Xi doesn't want to make this decision because he's still hoping that next year, during the Party Congress, somehow he'll get a fourth term. But the only way you can do that is by not making a mistake. I think letting U.S. corporations into the country to sell stablecoins, different factions will pounce on that.

It seems like the entire world is in a stalemate right now. It seems like things aren't progressing. Look, look, I made a prediction that there'll be a grand bargain between China and the United States, where basically China agrees to open up its financial markets, and the United States tells China we won't deal with Taiwan. We won't support Taiwanese independence. It basically creates a pathway for Taiwan and China to unify in the next ten years.

I think, as things unfold, it seems I'm wrong about this prediction. It's possible in two, three months' time things will change, but it seems right now that I'm on track to be wrong. If I'm wrong, I'm always asking myself, why am I wrong? I think I'm wrong because no one's in charge of China right now, so no decision can be made. That's why you have this slow death.

## AI, Russia, and the possibility of conflict

### Can AI and urban planning be used for the betterment of humanity?

I think that the idea that people will use AI for the common good is just ridiculous. The logic is very, very, very, very simple. For AI to be effective, you need economies of scale. You need to concentrate power. What we know is, in an institution, the more power you give it, the less empathy it has, the more top-down it becomes.

The classic example is city planning. I'm not sure if you've read about Jane Jacobs. If you read Jane Jacobs, her book The Death and Life of Great American Cities , it's a wonderful book. Why is it her ideas never became popular? Instead, you have someone like Robert Moses, who was probably the most famous urban planner of the 20th century. Why did he become so dominant? The answer is that's how power works. You put powerful people together, and you give them a blueprint. They understand what a blueprint is, and they understand how to implement the blueprint. But if you talk to them about human creativity and human diversity and human spirituality, they're like, what the—man, get out of here.

People in power are psychopaths. People in power are not very imaginative. They see the world in a very top-down way. The idea that we will use AI for the common good is just complete nonsense. If you have access to AI, it means you're a really powerful person. If you're a very powerful person, you're going to see the world in a very limited, very simplistic, very narrow manner.

### Why does Xi keep invoking the Thucydides Trap?

Audience: Something that I found interesting about the summit between Trump and Xi is that Xi once again invoked the Thucydides Trap. Response: Certain things to appreciate: the Thucydides Trap is a book written by a Harvard historian called Graham Allison. Graham Allison is Xi Jinping's favorite historian. It's flattering for the Chinese to think that they could potentially replace the United States one day.

It's paying homage to his friend Graham Allison.
